10.52(1)  Except when a person is before the Court as described in
subrule (3)(a)(ii) or (v), before an order declaring a person in civil
contempt of Court is made, notice of the application in Form 27 for
a declaration of civil contempt must be served on the person in the
same manner as a commencement document.
(2)  If a lawyer accepts service of a notice of an application seeking
an order declaring the lawyer’s client to be in civil contempt of
Court, the lawyer must notify the client of the notice as soon as
practicable after being served.
(3)  A judge may declare a person to be in civil contempt of Court
if
(a) the person, without reasonable excuse,
(i) does not comply with an order, other than an order to
pay money, that has been served in accordance with
the rules for service of commencement documents or
of which the person has actual knowledge,
(ii) is before the Court and engages in conduct that
warrants a declaration of civil contempt of Court,
(iii) does not comply with an order served on the person,
or an order of which the person has actual
knowledge, to appear before the Court to show cause
why the person should not be declared to be in civil
contempt of Court,
(iv) does not comply with an order served on the person,
or an order of which the person has actual
knowledge, to attend for questioning under these
rules or to answer questions the person is ordered by
the Court to answer,
(v) is a witness in an application or at trial and refuses to
be sworn or refuses to answer proper questions, or
(vi) does not perform or observe the terms of an
undertaking given to the Court,
or
(b) an enactment so provides.

BOOK_A.commentary:
A. Procedure and Object²
A vital step to maintain peace order and good government is the right and power of courts
to enforce their rulings, and maintain and protect the dignity and respect of the courts and their
proceedings. The power to do that by contempt proceedings is inherent. Compliance (coercion) is
one aim; so is punishment.³
The topic is important, because in many cases where any order has
been disobeyed, the real intention of the innocent party (and even of the court) is not to punish,
but to use contempt as the only real means of enforcing compliance with the order.⁴
Duties under a court order are owed to the court, not to the opponent.⁵
Rule 10.52(1), (2) deals with the procedure applicable on applications for contempt.⁶
There is
not much difference between the procedure on a contempt application and the procedure on any
other application.⁷
An application for someone to show cause why he or she should not be held in contempt of
court sets up a two-stage process (which Rr.10.51 and 10.52 also set. )⁸
Contempt applications should ordinarily be heard promptly.⁹
But usually great urgency is not
present, and then the Attorney-General or a party should start proceedings; the court itself should
not.¹⁰
In an urgent case such as a witness’ refusing to answer questions in open court, it will be

proper for the court to begin contempt proceedings itself at once. But unless there are special
circumstances, the court should not go on at once to convict and sentence, especially if there is a
jury which may be inﬂuenced by that conviction when deciding the main case.¹
B. Notice
See also R.11.17. Alberta courts have held that care must be taken with notice in two respects:
1. Just as under administrative law or criminal procedure, the person accused of contempt
or who is possibly to be punished for it²
must have clear and precise advance notice of
exactly what wrong-doing is alleged against him or her;³
and a chance to respond with
excuses, argument or evidence;⁴
and
2. There must be personal notice of the application to that person. Of course it is sufﬁcient
that the party alleged to be in contempt get personal notice in some manner; it does not
have to be personal service to effect that.⁵
Service of contempt applications, other than
those in the face of the court, may occur:
a. as agreed in a contract;
b. by personal service or recorded mail addressed to the individual;
c. by service on an individual’s lawyer, if they are acting for the individual and
accept service in writing; or
d. by leaving a copy with the individual’s lawyer of record, ofﬁce or other designated
address, or by recorded mail to the lawyer at the lawyer’s ofﬁce (¶ 13) ;
A determination of whether notice was sufﬁcient for a contempt application is for the
judge hearing the application to decide.⁶
If counsel is served and shows up on the return
of the contempt motion, what he or she says about notice is admissible evidence, e. g.
that the notice was sent on to the client. The court may then infer that the client had
actual notice.⁷
Indeed, proof of service on the solicitor of record shifts the onus to the

client to show that he did not get notice of the motion.¹
If the respondent or properly-
instructed counsel for him or her turns up for the application, that is likely to quell any
lingering concerns about service or notice, and there should be actual reason if fear of
lack of notice is to continue.²
Proceeding ex parte³
is cured if the party appears later and
the whole matter is heard afresh on the merits.⁴
C. Evidence
It is highly probable that civil contempt is considered a ﬁnal matter, so that the afﬁdavits
relied on to have the court ﬁnd contempt cannot contain hearsay.⁵
Double hearsay is likely to be
rejected.⁶
But certiﬁed copies of ofﬁcial documents, or proper secondary evidence of documents,
are permissible.⁷
The phrase “show cause” is misleading; the onus of proof is not on the person accused of
contempt.⁸
The party alleging contempt has the persuasive burden of proof, and the duty to give
or cite evidence, before the topic of reasonable excuse comes up.⁹
If contempt is shown, the onus lies on the offender to show that he has purged his contempt.¹⁰
Once the basic elements of contempt are proved, the evidential burden shifts to the accused
person to raise a reasonable doubt about some valid excuse for not obeying?¹¹
The precise nature
of the burden of proof about an adequate excuse for one's non-obedience is unclear.¹²
Even civil contempt must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt,¹³
as to both the actus reus and
mens rea.¹⁴
Proof that one knew of an order which one disobeyed, must be beyond a reasonable

doubt.¹
The party seeking contempt must prove disobedience of a clear unequivocal duty, known
to the person accused, and (ordinarily) intentional failure to comply.²
Contempt cannot be proved
by afﬁdavits which conﬂict on material questions.³
Reversal of onus may not be fatal if proof is
clear.⁴
The person accused of contempt cannot rely on mere factual assertions, and needs sworn
evidence.⁵
Like the party applying, he or she cannot rely on hearsay.⁶
The applicant should not plan or try to attack the respondent's credibility, yet have the
application to ﬁnd contempt heard in chambers without live evidence.⁷
But where the question is contempt in court, the Court of Appeal can act on its own knowledge
of that event.⁸
Admitting evidence potentially more prejudicial than probative, on a contempt hearing, is not
correct, but is not fatal, if the prejudicial parts were not relied on by the judge trying contempt, so
there was no effect on the result.⁹
Reasonable excuse for the accused person’s behavior is still a consideration and goes to guilt,
not just to liability.¹⁰
The reference in subrule (3) to “reasonable excuse” does remove either burden
of proof from the party alleging contempt. The court can presume that the accused person acted
knowing the facts, unless the latter gives some evidence, for only he or she knew what belief or
grounds for it he or she had.¹¹
D. Slips and Technicalities
A number of older cases suggested that the procedure for contempt is very strict, and that
small defects may derail the application. It is true that the matter is important, and that a court
should not put someone in prison where there may have been a serious procedural defect in the
process which got him or her there. But to ignore all the normal rules of civil procedure and the
normal slip Rules, and to rely on a technicality which in fact worked no real injustice, is wrong in
principle and ﬂouts many important Rules of Court. Why one would want to do that in favour of a
party who was (for example) disobeying a court order, and not do it for an honest litigant, is very
unclear.¹²
For example, notice how some curtailment of the right to cross-examine was not fatal in
the United Nurses case.¹³

E. Discretion and Procedure
See also Parts L and M below.
Now in Alberta contempt of court is a legislated topic, not an equitable one, and its origins are
common law, even though R.10.52(3) uses the word “declaration”. It is a quasi-criminal offence.
Equitable principles do not apply.¹
A judge has a discretion not to proceed with a complaint of contempt of court.²
So a technical
contempt may lead to no ﬁnding of contempt if the disobedient person was in good faith and took
reasonable steps to comply.³
A chambers judge can refuse to proceed with a contempt motion
involving a receiver, where it is not the right way to decide the real dispute, which is whether the
receiver is entitled to do what he proposes to do.⁴
The courts are critical of contempt motions
brought on slight or technical grounds.⁵
Where misconduct is shown but falls short of proving
contempt, the court can make other orders necessary to achieve justice.⁶
The reference in R.10.52(3) to absence of “reasonable excuse” makes the contempt power
highly discretionary, and it should not be used routinely to get compliance with court orders, and
is a last resort, especially in family law cases, even more so if custody is involved?⁷
Going into bankruptcy does not absolve one from a duty to obey a court order, nor bar or
satisfy contempt proceedings.⁸
Nor is being arrested on the scene and jailed over the weekend
until release, punishment for contempt, nor a purging of contempt, nor double punishment.⁹
The court can rehear a contempt ﬁnding and set it aside.¹⁰
Much harm is done by trying to sever parts of a contempt application and hear them on
another date or by another procedure.¹¹
For one thing, delay is bad where orders are being ﬂouted,
even if some issues are complex, and doubly so if the contempts are ongoing or threatened with
repetition, not historical.¹²
Usually contempt hearings are split into liability and penalty phases, and once the ﬁrst is
ﬁnished, during the second it is usually too late to reopen the liability issue.¹³
Compliance with

the order, or new facts just learned, might be an exception. Evidence obtainable earlier by due
diligence is not enough, as splitting one's case or holding back evidence is to be deterred.¹
F. Intent and Efforts
Only general mens rea is necessary for contempt;²
and for many types of contempt,
carelessness sufﬁces. For example, one ordered by a court to do something has a duty of diligence
and care to observe the order.³
Where a clear undertaking is given on questioning (examination
for discovery) to produce a certain document, best efforts exerted are not enough excuse for non-
compliance to avoid a ﬁnding of contempt.⁴
Intent to disobey is unnecessary.⁵
So it is enough to prove an intentional act or omission which
in fact breaches a clear order or court process of which the accused had notice.⁶
Direct knowledge
of the order is not needed if wilful blindness is proved.⁷
Error of law or acting on legal advice is not a defence.⁸
Nor is delegation to subordinates.⁹
It is
not an excuse that one’s lawyer was tied up or busy.¹⁰
A person ordered to do something can take
a little time to consider how, but cannot weigh competing considerations as to whether to obey.¹¹

Nor is it a defence, that the parties had agreed to stop obeying an order,¹
nor are prior conﬂicting
commitments.²
Though serious illness might be a defence, weak or vague evidence about illness
is not enough excuse.³
On what is a "reasonable excuse" (defence), see Imp. Finishing.⁴
On the other hand, reasonable excuse is relevant to more than just penalty. If the person
accused took reasonable steps to obey and acted in good faith, the judge has a discretion not to
convict, in order to avoid an injustice.⁵
Negligence is of course usually less blameworthy than deliberate disobedience.⁶
G. Jurisdiction and Error
Superior courts have full jurisdiction over allegations of contempt of court, even for acts before
a judge of the Alberta Court of Justice. “Competent jurisdiction” refers to what existed before
the Charter, and is not conﬁned to Charter issues. If one judge of the Alberta Court of Justice
is involved in the matters, she may and should refer the contempt matter to another judge. If the
Crown takes over the prosecution of contempt, it should then go to a superior court judge.⁷
It is well settled that an order of a superior court is never a nullity, and it is no defence to
contempt that the order disobeyed had been given as a result of some error or unfairness in
procedure or substance.⁸
Even if it was later upset on appeal.⁹
Violation of a known clear order
is contempt of court. It is no answer to contempt that the order itself was improper or should not
have been granted. It is valid and enforceable unless and until set aside.¹⁰
Nor is it an excuse that
the court order created a safety hazard, nor that the person disobeying is aboriginal.¹¹
Semble if a court has jurisdiction over a suit (e. g. by the respondent’s attornment), it has
jurisdiction to hear an application for contempt by disobeying the court’s directions.¹²

Nor is default or disobedience by one’s opponent an excuse.¹
Bad conduct of the opposing
party is irrelevant to contempt by this party, unless the opposing party actually impeded this
party’s performance of his or her duties and so led to the contemptuous act or omission.²
But it is not contempt not to obey an order which has already expired; and doubt whether it
has, can bar contempt.³
Our courts can order disclosure of foreign assets, so lack of jurisdiction
to make the order does not arise on a motion for contempt by nondisclosure.⁴
A party might get the court’s permission to withdraw an ill-advised undertaking, but only if the
party seeks that by a prompt application, not as an attempted defence to a much later contempt
motion.⁵
A bankruptcy Registrar can ﬁnd and punish contempt, but not imprison.⁶
Parliament purported to give youth courts exclusive jurisdiction over ex facie contempt by
youths. The grant does not violate s.96 of the Constitution, but the exclusivity does: the grant is
not exclusive.⁷
H. Disobeying Court Orders⁸
1. Introduction
The most common type of contempt of court is disobeying, or interfering with observance of,
a court order⁹
(except failure to pay money).¹⁰
On disobeying an erroneous court order, see R.10.52n. G, and the C. P. E. , Chapter 56, Part
M.3 and Chapter 62, Part P.3.
This is especially bad when done by a lawyer.¹¹

Respect for the court’s dignity, authority, and processes, is vital. Overlooking intentional
breaches of court orders erodes respect for the proper administration of justice. Especially where
the disobedience was not a momentary lapse of judgment amidst proper conduct.¹
2. Intent and Knowledge
Bad intent, or special mens rea, or intent to disobey or to harm, is not necessary for contempt.
It is enough to know the act and know²
of the contrary court injunction.³
There must be proof
beyond a reasonable doubt that the person accused had actual knowledge of the order which was
not obeyed.⁴
That the act done might not ultimately gain a beneﬁt is no defence to contempt, if it is
done with knowledge of an order to the contrary: trying to obstruct justice by interference with an
order (not yet in effect) is enough.⁵
Even in child custody matters, there is no room for self-help.⁶
Disobeying an arbitration award is not, without more, contempt.⁷
Even if before the arbitration the
court said that any later award would be deemed an order of the court, and then it approved this
award?⁸
Contempt by disobedience includes an inferior tribunal’s order which by statute has been
ﬁled in King's Bench and is enforceable as a King's Bench order would be.⁹
Claiming to have no key to the residence she owned, and so being unable to give one to
the realtor, despite an order to cooperate in selling the home, was either simple refusal, or was
engineering key custody so she could state she had no key, and was held to be in contempt of
court. She had a legal right to a key.¹⁰
People are to obey the spirit of court orders, but ambiguity in the relevant part of the order may
be a defence to a contempt charge.¹¹

Being over-busy is no excuse.¹
That the person who got the order had poor motives is
irrelevant.²
To be guilty, one has to know of the order or court process.³
3. Those Liable
Who can be liable for disobedience of an order is a little complicated. But the general rule is
that anyone who knowingly assists in interfering with the working of an order is guilty of contempt,
even if he or she is not a party to the suit and not named in the injunction.⁴
If one is named by
the court and the injunction is mandatory, one can be liable for contempt if one does nothing,
carelessly assuming that others will perform.⁵
Or tells one's opponent to do the work himself, and
hands him the source information and tells him to do the searching in it.⁶
It is contempt to disobey
directions of a pre-trial conference judge, and to refuse to cooperate at the last moment.⁷
Foreign
secrecy laws do not excuse disobeying a court order for better discovery.⁸
4. Miscellaneous
On reasonable excuse and burden of proof, see notes C and F above.
There is a discussion of repeatedly doing what the court had forbidden and failing to do what
it had ordered.⁹
The idea that the harm had already occurred, was a defence, was rejected.¹⁰
A continuing failure to obey a mandatory order (e. g. to produce items) is not a continuing
contempt allowing repeated convictions, nor allowing additions to an existing ﬁxed-length jail
sentence. A new conviction requires a new actus reus.¹¹
But if the injunction is negative, a new
act is a new actus reus.¹²
That the wrongful act has since become irrevocable, or that one has a conﬂicting duty, is
no excuse. There are better ways to deal with such a conﬂict.¹³
Claiming to have no key to the
residence which the respondent owned, and so being unable to give one to the realtor, despite a
court order to cooperate in selling the home, was either simple refusal, or was engineering key
custody so she could state she had no key, and was contempt. She had a legal right to get a key.¹⁴

Failure to obey an order to pay money into court is not an "order to pay money" under R.
10.52(3) (a) (i).¹
Nor is failure to pay money into one’s solicitor’s trust account, or to another
stakeholder, nor an order to give an accounting and pay the balance.²
I. Non-Attendance
A lawyer’s failure to appear in court despite a direction to do so, can be contempt.³
Failure to show up as a witness⁴
at questioning (examination for discovery) or failure to ﬁle an
afﬁdavit of documents, under the Rules or an appointment, is no longer itself contempt; the Rule
now requires that an order be obtained and breached to constitute contempt.⁵
What remedy ﬂows
from that is more a matter of civil procedure than it is one of punishing contempt.
In many situations, the court is more concerned to aid the innocent party by securing
enforcement of the duty to attend or give discovery, and to indemnify the innocent party’s
expenses.⁶
The Court of Appeal afﬁrmed an order that a plaintiff who would not reveal how
an accident happened, nor come to examinations for discovery, not be able to set the matter
down for trial until he did submit to examinations for discovery. There was doubt that the plaintiff
wanted to go to trial. Credibility was a live issue.⁷
A corporate defendant’s representative came to
examination for discovery uninformed and not ready to answer questions, even after a hiatus and
a warning in writing. It could be contempt in another case.⁸
It is not a defence to contempt that one’s lawyer was tied up or busy, so one did not come.⁹
The practice of not attending court, but faxing a request for adjournment the day before, was
criticized and did not work here.¹⁰
J. Undertakings
Breach of an undertaking to the court is contempt, and such undertakings have much the
same effect as court orders.¹¹
They are often given in lieu of injunctions, or as a condition of
getting an injunction or other interlocutory relief. Some undertakings are often implied, such as
the undertaking to pay damages caused by a wrongly-granted interlocutory injunction which one
has obtained, or the undertaking not to make collateral use of information one has got through the
discovery process.¹²
The same liability for contempt attaches to persons whose property is seized
for distress or to enforce a judgment, but are left in possession of the property, by the seizing
bailiff.¹³

Long failure to answer the undertakings on questioning (examination for discovery), despite an
order to do so, may lead to a ﬁnding of contempt and striking out the defaulter’s pleadings.¹
Best
efforts are not enough compliance to avoid a ﬁnding of contempt.²
One who gave an undertaking
cannot unilaterally qualify or withdraw it, and if performance is impossible, sworn evidence of that
is necessary.³
An undertaking to pay costs is not determining costs; it is a separate matter.⁴
Courts have
always had the power to enforce undertakings to the court, by contempt proceedings. And if the
undertaking was to pay money, the court has no power to revoke or vary the undertaking, as there
is also a contract with the other party.⁵
The court also has inherent power to enforce undertakings by solicitors even if they are
not to the court and have nothing to do with litigation, e. g. trust conditions or undertakings in
conveyancing.⁶
K. Other Examples of Contempt
Besides those things speciﬁcally enumerated in R.10.52(3), many other things are contempt
of court at common law.⁷
Here are some examples:
1. deterring a witness from testifying,⁸
or deterring a party from going on with her suit or
defence, whether by bribes, threats, physical interference, or by a publicity campaign
such as biased and one-sided coverage in the media of a civil suit.⁹
That overlaps with
2. prejudicing a pending trial, especially a jury trial, by one-sided publicity or by publishing
inadmissible evidence such as a confession.¹⁰
A publication on the eve of a jury parole-
eligibility hearing was held not strong enough to be contempt, especially as most of the
contents were already known to the public.¹¹
And publication of facts likely admissible at
trial in a newspaper with little circulation in the relevant city, well before a jury would be
empanelled, is not contempt.¹²
3. publishing criticisms of the honesty or motives of the court;¹³
but it is permissible to say
that a decision which the court has already given is wrong, or stupid or ignorant, even if
in fact it is the criticism itself which is wrong, stupid or ignorant.
4. letting a court go through a whole hearing about whether to forbid an act, without revealing
that one had already committed the act.¹⁴
Failure by counsel to make full disclosure on an
ex parte motion may amount to contempt if deliberate.¹⁵

5. at some point disrespect for the court and its processes, and disrespectful speech, can
become contempt.¹
6. attempting to intimidate a court ofﬁcial.²
But breach of a Rule is not itself contempt, if there is no judge's order compelling obedience.
The court can often relieve against not obeying a Rule, especially if no prejudice results.³
L. Appellate Review
A decision that someone is guilty of contempt of court, before any court decision on penalty,
is a “decision” under R.14.8 and so can be appealed, and time to appeal guilt starts running.
Separate appeals from the guilt and the penalty are possible, and the fact that a single appeal is
also possible, does not stop time running from the ﬁnding of guilt. Contempt proceedings are often
bifurcated between the two.⁴
On appeal from a contempt ﬁnding, correctness is the test for questions of law, but otherwise
the standard is reasonableness.⁵
And palpable and overriding error for fact questions, or for mixed
questions or applying a legal standard to particular facts.⁶
A ﬁnding of civil contempt is factual and
is reviewed on appeal for palpable and overriding error.⁷
Was there no (or insufﬁcient) weight to
relevant considerations, or failure to consider some, or consideration of irrelevant considerations?
The Court of Appeal will not substitute its own discretion.⁸
M. Other Avenues to Punish or Enforce
Costs against a lawyer personally are another way for the courts to control abuse of process,
working in parallel with contempt and with a Law Society's punishments (and contempt is also an
inherent court power). But the sanctions are not mutually exclusive, and might even be imposed
concurrently for the same misconduct.⁹
Which remedy to adopt when a lawyer is guilty of abuse
of process depends in part on the consequences, as contempt has strict procedures and stricter
standard of proof, so in a given case a court may opt for personal costs instead of contempt.¹⁰
The authority of the court over a solicitor is preventative, to ensure fair trial and justice, but the
Law Society acts reactively, and each body has its own role, so the court need not rely on the
Law Society to oversee and sanction conduct before the court.¹¹
Usually personal costs are a less
harsh penalty or shorter duration than contempt or professional discipline by the Law Society.¹²

Section 127 of the Criminal Code can be used against someone defying an interlocutory
injunction. The exception in s.127 only applies to a speciﬁc express statutory procedure, e. g.
deﬁning contempt and its penalty. Rules of Court setting penalty or procedure do not trigger that
exception, if the contempt order would be under the Rule or the court’s inherent power.¹
A lawyer can be sanctioned by his or her professional organization for having written a
disrespectful, insulting letter to a judge, and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms does
not bar such discipline.²
Non-payment of costs is not contempt because of the exception for "an order to pay money" in
R.10.52(3) (a) (i). But noncompliance with a child access order alleging unwillingness of the child
permits the Court to direct an intervention.³

commentary.text:
Rule 10.52 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Schitthelm v. Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, 2013 CarswellAlta 239, 557 A.R. 151, 278 C.R.R. (2d) 235, Justice Yamauchi provided a comprehensive summary of the law regarding contempt. His Lordship said: B. — The Nature of the Contempt Power 19 Superior courts have the inherent jurisdiction to control the proceedings before them. For a court to operate effectively, it requires an ability to maintain order in its proceedings and ensure its directions are followed. This is part of the rule of law. 20 Courts have differentiated between contempt of a civil nature and contempt of a criminal nature: see e.g. Poje v. British Columbia (Attorney General), [1953] 1 SCR 516 at 517 [Poje]; United Nurses of Alberta v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 SCR 901 at 931 [United Nurses]; Chiang (Trustee of) v. Chiang, 2009 ONCA 3 at para 10, 93 OR (3d) 483 and Seaward v. Paterson, [1897] 1 Ch 545 at 555-56, 559. However, in Vidéotron Ltée v. Industries Microlec Products Électioniques Inc, [1992] 2 SCR 1065 at 1075 [Vidéotron], Gonthier J warns that “too great an insistence on the distinction between civil contempt and criminal contempt” could mask characteristics common to all types of contempt. In Pro Swing Inc v. Elta Golf Inc, 2006 SCC 52 at para 34, [2006] 2 SCR 612 [Pro Swing], the Supreme Court of Canada states that the decision in Vidéotron set “aside the distinction between the civil and criminal aspects” of contempt law. Why is this? As mentioned in R. v. Cohn (1984), 48 OR (2d) 65 at para 11 [Cohn]: … the [Criminal] Code does not specifically provide for or define any such offence nor does it set forth any procedure for the prosecution of such offence or any penalty following conviction therefor. Resort must be had to the common law for these matters. Contempt of court is a common law offence. Thus, contempt, whether of a criminal or civil nature derives from the same source, the common law. Certainly, the context in which each occurs might differ, and the results that flow from each might inform whether the contempt is “civil” or “criminal.” However, as noted in Halsbury's Laws of England, vol 22, 5th ed (London, UK: LexisNexis, 2012) at para 2, footnote 1 [citations omitted], “[t]he classification of contempts as criminal or civil has become progressively less important and has been described as ‘unhelpful and almost meaningless’ in the present day”. 21 Vidéotron and Pro Swing indicate that contempt should not be looked at as merely “civil or “criminal” in nature, because all contempt has a public aspect and is of a “quasi-criminal nature”: Pro Swing at para 36. 22 While courts have held that civil contempt is generally coercive in nature and criminal contempt punitive in nature, this Court is not convinced that the procedural rights that attach to contempt proceedings and the Charter's applicability to them change merely because of the way in which one classifies the contempt. In all cases, courts must examine the particular facts before them and determine the procedures that natural justice and the Charter require. C. — Charter Applicability 23 The Charter is engaged when a person's liberty is at risk: see e.g. Re BC Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 SCR 486. In a contempt application, a person's liberty may be at risk: Rules rr 10.53(1)(a)–(c). Is the Charter engaged when a person faces a finding that they are in civil contempt pursuant to the Rules? … 25 Has a person who is alleged to have committed civil contempt been “charged” with anything? In Cohn at 75–76, the Ontario Court of Appeal said: The heading which precedes s. 11 of the Charter reads: “Proceedings in criminal and penal matters”. The portion of s. 11 which determines in the first instance the persons who may derive the benefit thereof is the first line which states: “Any person charged with an offence has the right …”. The heading to s. 11 makes it clear that s. 11 of the Charter applies to an offence although it may not be, strictly speaking, a criminal matter. It is sufficient if it is a penal matter. Even if contempt proceedings are not properly characterized as criminal matters, there can be no doubt that they must, at the very least, be characterized as penal matters. The word “penal” as used in the heading undoubtedly bears the dictionary meaning “of, pertaining to or relating to punishment”. It is the power to punish for contempt of court which is expressly preserved by s. 8 of the Criminal Code and, as previously stated, I am of the view that the citation for contempt of court constitutes the charging of an offence within the meaning of s. 11. It follows, therefore, that s. 11(c) and (d) of the Charter are applicable to contempt of court proceedings. 26 While one might think that, in a civil matter, the party making the application to have the court find the other party in civil contempt simply wants to have the court order enforced for its benefit, there can be no doubt that Rules rr 10.53(1)(b) and 10.53(1)(c) are penal in nature. The spectre of that punishment alone makes the Rules that govern civil contempt subject to the Charter, or at least some of its provisions. See e.g. R. v. Winter (1986), 72 AR 164 at para 9 [Winter], where the Alberta Court of Appeal chose not to follow a decision of the Québec Superior Court in Attorney-General of Quebec v. Laurendeau (1982), 3 CCC (3d) 250, which held that a person cited for contempt was not “charged” with an offence within the meaning of Charter s 11. In Placentia-St. Mary's Roman Catholic School Board v. Newfoundland Association of Public Employees, Local 5802 (1986), 60 Nfld & PEIR 350 at para 4 (Nfld SC (TD)), Steele J said “[t]he penalty for contempt of court may involve a fine or committal to jail and is therefore a punishment affecting the liberty of the person. Consequently contempt proceedings may have definite overtones of a criminal nature.” At paragraph 5, Steele J went on to quote, with agreement, the following passage from Nigel Lowe & Sir Gordon Borrie, Borrie & Lowe's Law of Contempt, 2nd ed (London, UK: Butterworths, 1983) at 393, where the authors said: Although this aspect of contempt is designated civil, because of the penal sanctions, it has been said to “partake of a criminal nature” and many of the rules that normally apply when seeking to prove an accused guilty of a crime, apply when seeking to show that the defendant has committed civil contempt. It also means that the rules safeguarding contemners'[sic] rights must be strictly complied with. [Footnotes omitted.] 27 Even if one concedes that Charter rights are engaged, does this provide a complete answer to the question concerning the procedures a court must use in contempt proceedings? The Charter itself comes with built-in limits. Charter s 7 provides that every right contained in that section is subject to restrictions that are in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. As well, every Charter right can be limited by engaging Charter s 1, which provides for “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” Indeed, in Winter at para 12, the Alberta Court of Appeal found the instanter procedure which the trial judge used to find the accused in contempt was justified under Charter s. 1. 28 In a civil contempt proceeding, the court may not discard the alleged contemnor's rights. The court must, however, carefully balance those rights against those of the party who alleges that the alleged contemnor has committed civil contempt. Above all, when a court considers the procedural requirements that are engaged in a civil contempt proceeding, it must ensure that the alleged contemnor is not found to have committed contempt without adequate proof of culpability. This informs all aspects of contempt procedure. 29 The procedure required to address the competing interests in contempt applications will not always remain constant; each case depends on its particular facts. D. — Procedure 30 In R. v. K(B), [1995] 4 SCR 186 at para 11 [K(B)], Lamer CJ said: In order to simplify matters, it is my opinion that we should use the notion of citing in contempt, not as an expression of a finding of contempt but instead, as a method of providing the accused with notice that he or she has been contemptuous and will be required to show cause why they should not be held in contempt. 31 While the cases that deal with criminal contempt are distinguishable from civil contempt under the Rules, they are instructive in assisting the courts in fashioning a procedure to use when considering an allegation of civil contempt. What emerges from those cases, and what natural justice and the Charter require, is a three-stage procedure: citing the person in contempt of the court, conviction and sentencing. Under the Rules, those stages are specifically outlined as follows: Citing the person in contempt of the court: Rules rr 10.52(1) and 10.52(2) require the accuser provide the alleged contemnor with notice of the application for a declaration of civil contempt; Conviction: Rules r 10.52(3) allows the judge to “declare” the alleged contemnor to be in civil contempt; Sentencing: Rules r 10.53 outlines the “penalties” and “sanctions” the judge might impose on the contemnor. 32 Each stage should be separated, unless there is an urgent and imperative reason why the stages should be collapsed so the procedure can be expedited: R. v. Arradi, 2003 SCC 23 at para 30, [2003] 1 SCR 280 [Arradi]; Doobay v. Diamond, 2012 ONCA 580 at para 40, leave to appeal to SCC requested. Types of Contempt and Powers in Relation Thereto (i)—Civil contempt At the outset I propose to make some general remarks concerning contempt of Court so that others besides those appearing here today will have a more precise knowledge of what consequence can flow from the disobedience of lawful orders of the Supreme Court of this or any other Province in this country. That disobedience may amount to civil contempt or criminal contempt. The parties to a civil action, such as here, can apply on motion for an order for civil contempt where an order of the Court has not been obeyed. Our Rules of Court set out the penalties that may be imposed for civil contempt. Those penalties are set forth in Rule 704. It says: 704. Every person in civil contempt is liable to any one or more of the following: (a) imprisonment until he has purged his contempt; (b) imprisonment for one year; (c) a fine of $1,000 and in default of payment thereof, to imprisonment for one year; and other sanctions such as striking out pleadings. (ii)—Criminal contempt But the Criminal Code of Canada contains a provision, s. 116, which also covers the situation. Section 116 of the Criminal Code says: 116. Every one who, without lawful excuse, disobeys a lawful order made by a court of justice or by a person or body of persons authorized by any Act to make or give the order, other than an order for the payment of money is, unless some penalty or punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law, guilty of (a) an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years; or (b) an offence punishable on summary conviction. All that means is that the Attorney-General of this Province or any other Province, being the chief law enforcement officer, can prefer an indictment against people who disobey lawful orders of the Court. Foothills Provincial General Hospital v. Broad (1976), 57 D.L.R. (3d) 758 (Alta. T.D.), at 759, per Quigley J. The equivalent section in the current Criminal Code is s. 127 which reads as follows: 127. (1) Every one who, without lawful excuse, disobeys a lawful order made by a court of justice or by a person or body of persons authorized by any Act to make or give the order, other than an order for the payment of money, is, unless a punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law, guilty of (a) an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years; or (b) an offence punishable on summary conviction. (2) Where the order referred to in subsection (1) was made in proceedings instituted at the instance of the Government of Canada and conducted by or on behalf of that Government, any proceedings in respect of a contravention of or conspiracy to contravene that order may be instituted and conducted in like manner. 4. Contempt Proceeding Instituted by Court However, and this is little known I think outside of legal circles—there is a much more awesome power resting in the Court itself, that is in the Supreme Court. The Court may ex mero motu, that is of its motion, institute proceedings for criminal contempt and this contempt, if confirmed, permits penalties that are virtually unlimited. And that power has come down through the ages and rests in every Court of superior jurisdiction. So it would be folly for any one to assume that contempt proceedings depend on the parties to the action or that one must await the application of the Attorney-General. The inherent power of the Court to institute contempt proceedings is always there and it does not only reside in the justice of the Court whose order has been disobeyed. Any member of the Supreme Court of Alberta may, of his own motion, institute such proceedings, and at this moment with the evidence before me and the admissions before me I have the power to change these proceedings from civil contempt to one of criminal contempt, and if I do that and if criminal contempt is found, I will also have the power as a member of this Court to impose virtually any penalty. Foothills Provincial General Hospital v. Broad (1976), 57 D.L.R. (3d) 758 (Alta. T.D.), at 759-60, per Quigley J. And Cooke J. said: I find that the breaches of the express terms of the order in its original and amended form constitute contempt. Is that contempt civil or criminal in its nature? This question was canvassed at length by my brother Cavanagh in the case of Gainers Inc. v. United Food and Commercial Workers Union et al. (September 4, 1986), (unreported), action 8603 12647). He cites an unreported decision of the British Columbia Supreme Court, J.C. Kerkoff and Sons Construction Ltd. v. The distinction being broadly one between disobedience to orders or writs made or issued in civil actions (civil contempts) and contumacious behaviour or behaviour which tends to publicly depreciate the authority of the court or the administration of justice (criminal contempts). Where the public nature of the defiance of a civil order brings the administration of justice into scorn, the offence is a criminal contempt. Zeidler Forest Industries Ltd. v. [The learned trial judge] proceeded to try the matter himself forthwith and started by summarizing the “facts” as taken by him from the file of the defendant solicitor. He then invited counsel for [the lawyers] to consider whether they wished to testify … It is not necessary to consider in detail the numerous procedural defects apparent on the face of this record. Though there was in this case no urgent need to protect the administration of justice by an immediate hearing, the full matter proceeded at once. The judge found himself as the initiator of the proceeding, the prosecutor at the trial, the source of the evidence not given under oath and not subjected to cross-examination, and the judge of the issue. The accused persons were called upon to defend themselves immediately against allegations of wrong-doing which to this day have never been stated in so many words. We feel constrained to point out once again how undesirable it is, except in the most urgent situations, for the Court itself to initiate the contempt process. As Allen, J.A., said in Mathieson v. Mathieson, [1974] 5 W.W.R. 453, at 464–465: In other cases of contempt not committed in the face of the Court the most appropriate procedure appears to be … in the case of civil contempt either to permit the party affected or aggrieved by the contempt to move by Originating Notice or a Notice of Motion or to direct the Attorney General to take the matter in hand and proceed in such manner as he may see fit in the circumstances of the case. 5. Criminal versus Civil Contempt It is my view that a clear distinction exists between civil and criminal contempt and that the law of criminal contempt is sufficiently certain to meet the requirements of fundamental justice. The distinction between civil and criminal contempt rests in the concept of public defiance that accompanies criminal contempt. Both civil and criminal contempt of court rest on the power of the court to uphold its dignity and process. The rule of law is at the heart of our society; without it there can be neither peace, nor order nor good government. The rule of law is directly dependent on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect. To maintain their process and respect, courts since the 12th century have exercised the power to punish for contempt of court. These same courts found it necessary to distinguish between civil and criminal contempt. A person who simply breaches a court order, for example by failing to abide by visiting hours stipulated in a child custody order, is viewed as having committed civil contempt. However, when the element of public defiance of the court's process in a way calculated to lessen societal respect for the courts is added to the breach, it becomes criminal. This distinction emerges from Poje v. Attorney General for British Columbia, [1953] 1 S.C.R. 516, at p. 527, per Kellock J.: The context in which these incidents occurred, the large numbers of men involved and the public nature of the defiance of the order of the court transfer the conduct here in question from the realm of a mere civil contempt, such as an ordinary breach of injunction with respect to private rights in a patent or trade-mark, for example, into the realm of a public depreciation of the authority of the court tending to bring the administration of justice into scorn. [Emphasis added by McLachlin J.] What the courts have fastened on in this and other cases where criminal contempt has been found is the concept of public defiance that “transcends the limits of any dispute between particular litigants and constitutes an affront to the administration of justice as a whole”: B.C.G.E.U. v. British Columbia (Attorney General), supra, at p. 237, per Dickson C.J., Lamer, Wilson, La Forest, and L'Heureux-Dubé JJ. concurring. The gravamen of the offence is not actual or threatened injury to persons or property; other offences deal with those evils. The gravamen of the offence is rather the open, continuous and flagrant violation of a court order without regard for the effect that may have on the respect accorded to edicts of the court. U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901, at 931–32, per McLachlin J. for the majority. In R. v. Edmonton Sun (2003), 12 Alta. L.R. (4th) 6 (C.A.), McFadyen J.A. said at p. 19: Criminal contempt is, therefore, clearly aimed at punishing public acts which tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute and interfere with the due administration of justice. 6. Requirements to Prove Criminal Contempt To establish criminal contempt the Crown must prove that the accused defied or disobeyed a court order in a public way (the actus reus), with intent, knowledge or recklessness as to the fact that the public disobedience will tend to depreciate the authority of the court (the mens rea). The Crown must prove these elements beyond a reasonable doubt. As in other criminal offences, however, the necessary mens rea may be inferred from the circumstances. An open and public defiance of a court order will tend to depreciate the authority of the court. Therefore when it is clear the accused must have known his or her act of defiance will be public, it may be inferred that he or she was at least reckless as to whether the authority of the court would be brought into contempt. On the other hand, if the circumstances leave a reasonable doubt as to whether the breach was or should be expected to have this public quality, then the necessary mens rea would not be present and the accused would be acquitted, even if the matter in fact became public. While publicity is required for the offence, a civil contempt is not converted to a criminal contempt merely because it attracts publicity, as the union contends, but rather because it constitutes a public act of defiance of the court in circumstances where the accused knew, intended or was reckless as to the fact that the act would publicly bring the court into contempt. U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901 at 933. 7. Overview In Hover v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. (1999), 237 A.R. 30 (C.A.), Madam Justice Fruman gave the following summary of the law relating to contempt. At pp. 34-35, Her Ladyship said: Rule 702 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits the court to declare a person in civil contempt. Rule 703(a) clarifies that a person who “fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the court” is in civil contempt. Rule 704 provides that a person in civil contempt is liable to have his pleadings struck, his action dismissed and judgment entered against him. If contempt is found, the Chambers judge has a number of alternatives. He may, for example, require that another notice be given directing the party to attend and “show cause” why he should not be held in contempt. He may find the party in contempt but suspend the remedy for a period of time, to permit the party to comply with the court order and purge the contempt. He may find the party in contempt and impose a remedy which takes effect immediately. A person alleged to be in contempt must be given an opportunity to provide “an adequate excuse” for his disobedience of a court order. Personal service of the contempt motion on the litigant is not required. The Rules provide that personal service on a litigant is required only when the Rules expressly say so (rule 13(1)), or the document being served commences an action or proceeding (rule 14). As neither circumstance applies to contempt applications, service on a litigant's counsel is permitted (rule 26(1)). See also Harder v. Hater, [1975] 4 W.W.R. 765 (Alta. C.A.). The motion must however, come to the personal notice of the litigant who is being cited in contempt: Kin Franchising Ltd. v. Donco Ltd. (1993), 7 Alta. L.R. (3d) 313 (C.A.). Because of the serious consequences, caution should be exercised to the extent that the person cited in contempt “is given an opportunity to retain and instruct counsel”: 250242 Alberta Ltd. v. Sohal (1983), 44 A.R. 34 at pp. 38-39 (C.A.). The onus is on the applicant to prove that notice of the application has been given to the person accused of contempt. The best method is by proof of personal service, but there are other ways. If, for example, the notice of motion was served on counsel for the person cited in contempt, the applicant may rely on statements made by counsel: 354415 Alberta Ltd. et al. v. Qureshi (1992), 127 A.R. 148 at p. 151 (C.A.). Once the court is satisfied that adequate and proper notice has been given, the applicant may proceed with the contempt motion despite the absence of the party alleged to be in contempt, or his legal representative. . . . . . The decision to find a party in contempt is within the chamber judge's discretion: Labour Relations Board (Sask.) v. Daschuk Lumber, [1976] 5 W.W.R. 562, (Sask. C.A.), at p. 565, as is the remedy and manner in which it is imposed. The standard of review is reasonableness: Russell Food Equipment (Calgary) Ltd. v. Valleyfield Investment Ltd. (1962), 40 W.W.R. (N.S.) 292 (Alta. T.D.). A reviewing court may not substitute its own discretion unless it finds that the Chambers judge did not give sufficient weight to relevant considerations; proceeded arbitrarily, on wrong principles or on an erroneous view of the facts; or there is likely to be a failure of justice (at p. 295). In Sulphur Experts Inc. v. O'Connell (2000), 279 A.R. 246 (Q.B.), Romaine J., when considering an application for an order declaring that the defendant O'Connell was in civil contempt for allegedly breaching an Anton Piller order, provided the following summary of what must be proven on such an application (at p. 252): In order to justify a finding of civil contempt under rule 703 of the Alberta Rules of Court, the plaintiff must show that the defendants failed, without adequate excuse, to obey the ex parte Anton Piller order. The plaintiff must establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendants were aware of the order and the civil contempt occurred. This is so because contempt of court is a serious matter of a criminal or quasi criminal nature. … Not only must the defendants be made aware of the order, but they must be aware of its substance. … There is no dispute that the postponement of compliance with an order can amount to contempt. … It is also conceded that the absence of intent to commit contempt is a mitigating but not an exculpatory factor. … In W. (S.) v. T. (K.) (2005), 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 57 (Q.B.), Lee J. discussed generally the concept of contempt. At pp. 64–65, his Lordship said: A person will be in civil contempt if he or she fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the Court. … Intention to disobey a Court order is not necessarily required for a finding of contempt, however, where someone is ordered to do something, he or she must use a sufficient degree of diligence to perform or have the act performed by someone else. … Contempt extends beyond the breach of a specific term in a Court order and can be found where the actions taken by a person are ‘desgined to obstruct the course of justice by thwarting or attempting to thwart a Court order’. … The purpose of the Court's civil contempt powers is to achieve compliance with Court orders and to uphold the Court's authority. … The sanction of contempt should be proportional to the personal responsibility of the person in contempt and to the seriousness of the contempt. … The decision to find a party in contempt and the remedy and manner in which it is imposed are all within the chambers judge's discretion. … 10. Shenner, 2024 ABCA 285, the Court said: [20]…[S]ervice of a contempt application may be effected pursuant to Rule 11.17…. … [35] While personal service of a contempt application is not required, the common law has generally required the application to come to the personal attention of the alleged contemnor: Shenner 2022 at para 17. As such, it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt … 12. Reasonable Excuse In Envacon Inc. v. 829693 Alberta Ltd., 2018 ABCA 313, 2018 CarswellAlta 2097, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 9, the Court of Appeal addressed the issue of “reasonable excuse” and how it factors into “intent”. The Court said: 30 In our view, reasonable excuse remains a consideration when determining whether there has been civil contempt pursuant to rule 10.52 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010. Reasonable excuse is not relegated to determining the proper penalty. Rule 10.52(3) states that a judge may declare a person to be in civil contempt if: (a) the person, without reasonable excuse, (i) does not comply with an order, other than an order to pay money, that has been served in accordance with the rules for service of commencement documents or of which the person has actual knowledge … [Emphasis added] 31 This rule is substantially the same as rule 703(1) of the repealed Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/68 (old Rules): Every person is in civil contempt who (a) fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the court, other than an order for the payment of money, … [Emphasis added] 32 Before Carey[Carey v. Laiken 2015 SCC 17] the words “without reasonable excuse” (or, under the old Rules, “without adequate excuse”) were part of the test for civil contempt. The leading Alberta case is Point on the Bow Development Ltd v William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775 at para 19, 405 AR 1 where the court listed the elements of contempt as “(1) an existing requirement of the court; (2) notice of the requirement to the person alleged to be in contempt; and (3) an intentional act (or failure to act) that constitutes a breach of the requirement”. These are the same requirements set out in Carey. … 34 Following Carey, Alberta courts have continued to incorporate the words “without reasonable excuse” into the test for civil contempt. For example, in Storage Capital (2) LP v 1288314 Alberta Ltd, 2018 ABQB 292 at para 27, 146 WCB (2d) 29, Shelley J adopted the three part test from Carey and added “without adequate excuse” as a “further qualifier to the third element”; see also Porter v Anytime Custom Mechanical Ltd, 2016 ABQB 322 at para 16, [2016] AWLD 3525. 35 There is another interpretation of Carey. The main issue in Carey was whether an alleged contemnor must have “contumacious” intent—that is, a desire to willfully disobey the court or to interfere with the administration of justice. The contemnor, Carey (a lawyer), was found to have breached an injunction that prohibited any person from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” the assets of one of his clients, including assets held in trust accounts. Carey breached the order by returning to his client funds that he had been holding in trust and argued that his professional duties as a lawyer required him to return the funds. He contended that while he had in fact breached the order, he did not intend to disobey the court or interfere with the administration of justice, and accordingly, he should not be found in contempt. The Supreme Court rejected this argument. Contumacious intent is not an essential element of contempt. It is not the intent to disobey the order that constitutes contempt, it is the disobedience itself: “all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice” (para 38). 36 We do not read Carey as changing the law that requires courts to look at reasonable excuse as an aspect of the test for finding contempt. Carey focusses primarily on the mens rea or the “mental element” of contempt: paras 28, 40–43. The Supreme Court found that once an alleged contemnor has acted, or failed to act, in contravention of a clear court order of which he or she had notice, no special mens rea in the form of contumacious intent need be proved. Thus, excuses (such as Carey's) that went to the motivation or the intention behind the breach did not affect the finding of contempt. We also reject the suggestion that Carey changed this approach and that reasonable excuse is only to be considered with respect to the penalty after a finding of contempt. 37 However, not all reasonable excuses are an element of mens rea. Reasonable excuses may also go to the actus reus of contempt. In order to be found in contempt, “the party allegedly in breach must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels” (Carey at para 35, emphasis added). Particularly in the case of mandatory orders, an alleged contemnor may argue that his or her failure to do what the court required was not intentional. In these cases, a finding of contempt will turn on whether the alleged contemnor did enough to bring about the result the court order required. This enquiry is distinct from the question of mens rea or contumacious intent, which was at issue in Carey. Thus, not all “reasonable excuses” encompassed by rule 10.52(3) are excluded by the Supreme Court's rejection of contumacious intent as an element of contempt. 38 Indeed, Cromwell J, writing for the Court in Carey at para 37, acknowledged that in some cases, an alleged contemnor who tries diligently to obey an order but fails may avoid a finding of contempt (citations omitted and emphasis added): [W]here an alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with the order, the judge entertaining a contempt motion generally retains some discretion to decline to make a finding of contempt … While I prefer not to delineate the full scope of this discretion, given that the issue was not argued before us, I wish to leave open the possibility that a judge may properly exercise his or her discretion to decline to impose a contempt finding where it would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case. 39 In such cases, the alleged contemnor in effect has a reasonable excuse for failing to comply. That excuse goes to the finding of contempt, and not to the remedy or penalty. 40 In our view, Carey is consistent with the possibility of a due diligence defence to a finding of contempt. On the facts of Carey a defence of due diligence was not possible. The order restraining Carey was prohibitory: it required him to refrain from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” funds belonging to his client. Carey intentionally did the act—the transfer—that contravened the order. The actus reus was clear. He chose not to obey the order. This differs from the situation where an alleged contemnor fails to comply with an order despite taking every reasonable step to do so. There may often be not much practical difference when the prima facie case of contempt is shown and the only evidence of the alleged excuse must be given by the alleged contemnor.
