Consequently, as a matter of tactics and prudence, in order to avoid a finding of contempt, the alleged contemnor may be compelled by the weight of adverse evidence establishing contempt, to put forward countervailing evidence either to provide a reasonable excuse or to prove that it did what was required of the order. 49 However, this is not a “shifting of a burden” because the alleged contemnor is not obliged to do anything. “The decision of a party to go forward with evidence because the risk of an adverse verdict is too great is not a question of law but a matter of common sense. Since the [alleged contemnor] is not required by law to do anything, this tactical decision to adduce evidence is not an evidential burden (using the definition in this text) and thus there is no shifting of the evidential burden:” Sopinka, Letterman & Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada, 4th ed. (Markham, Ont: LexisNexis Canada, 2014) at para 3.53 and cases cited therein. 50 In sum, the burden of proof both as to persuasion and the need for evidence is entirely on the party alleging contempt, and the standard is proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In the main, this is the approach advocated in Schitthelm except for its suggestion that there is an evidential burden on the alleged contemnor. There is no burden placed on the alleged contemnor at all. It follows that the competing approach in FIC Real Estate and adopted by the case management judge is incorrect. 13. Court Relying on Submissions of Counsel on issues of due diligence In Vavrek v. Varvek, 2019 ABCA 325, 2019 CarswellAlta 1897, [2019] A.J. No. 1195, in a family law dispute over child support, Ms. Vavrek applied for an order finding Mr. Vavrek in contempt of an order requiring Mr. Vavrek to supply certain financial information. The learned Chambers Judge, relying in part on submissions made by Mr. Vavrek's counsel that “an expert opinion would address [Ms. Vavrek's] concern and other issues relevant to a guideline income calculation”, refused to find Mr. Vavrek in contempt, and made another order requiring “the parties to take steps that would resolve the only issue in the litigation between them”. Ms. Vavrek appealed the order dismissing her contempt application. The Court of Appeal favourably commented on the learned Chambers Judge's reliance on submissions of counsel: [11] As pointed out by this Court in Envacon Inc v. 829693 Alberta Ltd, 2018 ABCA 313 at paras 40 to 41, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 98 (which was another case of alleged non-compliance with an order for discovery) the alleged contemnor is entitled to plead due diligence in the effort to comply in answer to the citation. Recognizing the possibility of such an answer is designed to encourage efforts to comply—which is an aim effectively recognized by Rule 10.52(3)(a) of the Rules of Court, AR 124/2010 as amended. [12]… The chambers judge had a discretion to exercise: Envacon at paras 59 to 60. In exercising that discretion, the chambers judge was entitled to rely upon the submissions of counsel as to whether there was a triable question of due diligence requiring a fuller hearing: compare R v Tymchyshyn, 2016 MBCA 73 at paras 14 to 20, 338 CCC (3d) 425, leave denied (2019) [2018] SCCA No 547 (QL) (SCC No. 38566) and cases (including from the Supreme Court) cited therein; see also R v Blackman, 2008 SCC 37 at paras 29 to 30, [2008] 2 SCR 298; R v Pires, 2005 SCC 66 at paras 8, 32 and 46, [2005] 3 SCR 343; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation v New Brunswick, 1996 CanLII 184 (SCC), [1996] 3 SCR 480 at para 72; R v Doonanco, 2019 ABCA 118 at para 142, 373 CCC 3d 275, under appeal as of right (SCC No 38577). [13] As noted in Doonanco, this procedural approach of relying on counsel submissions dates back at least to R v Dietrich, 1970 CanLII 377 (ON CA), [1970] 3 OR 725 as described in R v Sproule (1975), 1975 CanLII 1354 (ON CA), 26 CCC (2d) 92 at paras 23 to 25. And as these cases say, trial judges are entitled to proceed pragmatically to assess whether there are sufficient issues to warrant a fuller hearing. A fortiori, chambers judges should be given a similar margin of appreciation. Added to this is the considerable deference owed to chambers judges in dealing with family law cases: see eg Wild v Wild, 2019 ABCA 159 at paras 6 to 7, [2019] AJ No 513 (QL). Furthermore, counsel are officers of the court and are ethically bound to be forthright. To be sure, the same cannot be said for unrepresented parties and courts will necessarily be more circumspect there. There was no error on the part of the chambers judge to proceed as she did here. 14. Intent to Disobey Not Always Required In Michel v. Lafrentz (1998), 68 Alta. L.R. (3d) 140 (C.A.), a party to a lawsuit, who had been ordered to produce certain information, failed to do so. In hearing an application for an order declaring the defaulting party to be in contempt of court, Côté J.A. said, at pp. 144–45: It must not be thought that contempt of court always requires an intent to disobey the court, or even an intent to do an act which is in fact forbidden. Where someone is ordered by the court to do something, he or she must use a sufficient degree of diligence to perform, or to have the act performed … . . . . . Doubtless the person ordered to perform is not an insurer. Had an accidental fire suddenly destroyed his records, or his accountant been run over by a bus, likely either would excuse some delay, and maybe some temporary incompleteness, and there would not be contempt of court in the meantime. But it would not suffice to delegate the duty to the office boy. Nor did it suffice here to delegate the duty to a lawyer, or accountant, and not diarize or follow up on the matter. An order of a court to do an act requires reasonable care in doing the act personally, or in delegating the matter to suitable responsible persons, and then checking to see that it has been carried out in a prompt and proper fashion. That is doubly so when the final act required is an oath by the person ordered. Then he has to satisfy himself of the accuracy of the information before he signs and declares (or swears). Anything else would be perjury. 15. Notice Must Be Given of Specific Breach A citation for civil contempt is a matter strictissimi juris because it affects the liberty of the subject. The delict must be defined with particularity and proven beyond a reasonable doubt. In Re Pollard (1868), L.R. 2 P.C. 106, at 120 the formal report of the court is reported as saying: … no person should be punished for contempt of court, which is a criminal offence, unless the specific offence charged against him be distinctly stated, and an opportunity of answering it given to him, and … in the present case their Lordships are not satisfied that a distinct charge of the offence was stated. Northwest Territories Public Service Association v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner) (1980), 21 A.R. 1 at 17 (N.W.T. C.A.). In Letal v. Board of Education of Lakeland Roman Separate School District No. 150 (2000), 276 A.R. 130 (Q.B.), Verville J. discussed the concept of strictissimi juris (of the strictest right or law). At p. 139, his Lordship said: Further, the comment of the Newfoundland Court of Appeal in Iron Ore Co. of Canada v. United Steel Workers of America, Local 5795 and Dwyer et al. (1979), 20 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 27 … is helpful in understanding the purpose behind the “strictissimi juris” rule: “While the principle of ‘strictissimi juris’ undoubtedly applies, what it means in this particular instance is that the Court must be scrupulous in ensuring that the alleged contemnors, once brought before it, are fully aware of the charges against them which they are required to answer and, further, are given every opportunity to answer such charges. In the absence of any rules in our civil or criminal procedure dealing with contempt of court, this in my view is the way in which the ‘strictissimi juris’ principle must be applied to proceedings of this nature.’” 16. Nature of Contempt It will be noted from R. 703 that the only part of the definition which might apply to contempt committed in the face of the court is para. (c), that is to say, the refusal of a witness in any action or proceeding to be sworn or to affirm or answer proper questions. All of the other provisions clearly relate to contempt not in the face of the court … The justification for a court acting brevi manu and summarily in the case of contempt committed in the face of the court is, as pointed out in several cases, found in the fact that the contempt occurs in the presence of the court, which has full knowledge of what has occurred: see Laskin J. in the McKeown case … It does not have to look to any outside source for evidence of the occurrence or the nature thereof, and it is essential that the most prompt action be taken to prevent a disruption or disturbance of the course of justice. Even so opportunity appears almost always to be afforded to an accused person to offer an explanation or an apology before any drastic punishment is imposed. Mathieson v. Mathieson, [1974] 5 W.W.R. 453 at 467, 469 (Alta. C.A.). The Court of Appeal has noted that it is not necessary to find the breach of a specific term of a court order before contempt is found to exist. In Litterst v. Horrey (1995), 178 A.R. 216 (C.A.), Chief Justice Fraser, speaking for the court, said, at p. 219: Contempt of court extends beyond the breach of a specific term in a court order: Baxter Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada) Ltd., [1983] 2 S.C.R. 388 … It will be sufficient if the actions taken by the person alleged to be in contempt are designed to obstruct the course of justice by thwarting or attempting to thwart a court order. That is what Horrey has done in this case. Whether he succeeds in his ultimate objective is irrelevant. In Arrow-West Equipment Ltd. v. GDT Trading Ltd. (2006), 407 A.R. 129 (Alta. Q.B.), Acton J. said, at pp. 134-135: In my view, giving evidence knowing it to be false or intentionally destroying the subject matter of an action also constitutes contempt of Court.… The party accused of such contempt must be given notice of the particulars of the alleged contempt. In Berube v. Wingrowich (1999), 251 A.R. 128 (Q.B.), the court had ordered that the corporate respondent pay certain royalty funds into a lawyer's trust account during the course of the litigation. The monies were so paid, but on a subsequent request of the respondent, the lawyer paid the funds out of his trust account in contravention of the order. The Court found both the corporate respondent and the lawyer to be in contempt of court. At pp. 133–134, Veit J. said: Not every misbehaviour constitutes contempt of court. However, an intentional attempt to mislead the court is contempt of the court. In addition, the common law establishes that the intentional breach of a court order, even of a civil order between private litigants, is contempt of court. In this context, the court's contempt jurisdiction is not designed to assist one party or the other; rather, the court's power is to be exercised to uphold and nurture the rule of law, with a view to ensuring civil order by discouraging people from taking law into their own hands. Therefore, the intentional breach of the court's mandatory injunction to place a “royalty” into a trust account and to keep it there until further order is conduct that could be contempt of court. Lawyers are officers of the court, owing responsibilities to the court and the community as well as to their clients. While it may be a moot point whether lawyers are held to a higher standard than other advocates or other members of the public, it is clear that lawyers must behave, both in and out of court, according to the standards of their office. … As to the specific obligation to obey court orders, no one—including no lawyer—should place themselves in the position of assisting in breaches of valid court orders. … Lawyers are never mere agents, mere mouthpieces, for their clients. It will not avail a lawyer, in answer to a charge of impropriety, to say, “My client made me do it.” The representations from Mr. Wingrowich that he “pressed” Mr. Goldenberg [the lawyer] to pay monies out of a trust fund must therefore be ignored in considering whether Mr. Goldenberg's behaviour in this manner has been contemptuous. At the very least, it has been established beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Goldenberg did these two things: • with knowledge of the Consent Order … and without ensuring that Mr. Wingrowich was in fact attempting to implement the business evaluator's recommendation …, Mr. Goldenberg paid the royalty monies out of his trust account to Itlwork [the corporate respondent]; and • on March 9, 1999, he allowed the court to assume that the monies were still in his trust account, thereby both misleading the court and delaying any attempt to quickly replace the monies that he had paid out on March 5, 1999. Each of these actions constitutes contempt. I therefore find Mr. Goldenberg in contempt of court. Mr. Wingrowich's affidavit clearly establishes that he knew of the original mandatory injunction and that a stay of the order implementing the recommendations would require the monies in the trust account to remain there or to be immediately returned to the account. Despite this knowledge, he took the monies out of the trust account and has not returned them. Mr. Wingrowich pleads that there are many reasons why he should not have had to obey the consent order in the first place. The law is clear. People must obey a clear order of the court, even if the order is wrong, until the order is set aside. Mr. Wingrowich must obey the court's orders until the Court of Appeal sets those order aside. Because Goldenberg, Wingrowich and Itlwork acted in concert to breach the court order, they are jointly and severally responsible to return the monies forthwith to the credit of this action. … Veit J. then order that costs be paid forthwith on an indemnity basis. In subsequent proceedings [Berube v. Wingrowich (1999), 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 59 (Q.B.)], Veit J. reconsidered her decision and withdrew the contempt finding in relation to the breach of the court order, but reaffirmed her finding of contempt in relation to misleading the court. 17. A Breach of the Rules is not Contempt In Point on the Bow Development Ltd. v. William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd. (2006), 68 Alta. L.R. (4th) 308 (Alta. Q.B.); affirmed (2007) 78 Alta. L.R. (4th) 16 (Alta. C.A.)], Rooke J. said, at p. 323: … On the broader question, my view is that any breach of a Rule or enactment is not contempt in itself (in the absence of the Rule or enactment specifically so providing) unless so declared by a Court by a specific order or direction. Thus, mere failure to follow a Rule would not be contempt. Rather, the failure should, in the normal course, be the subject of a specific Court order….Failure to obey such an order, without adequate excuse, would, however be prima facie contempt, but only when once declared by further Court order. I note that Rule 703 does not deal with breach of the Rules, but only with “an order of the court”. Rule 703(1)(f) provides an exception where the Rule or enactment specifically makes a breach contempt. 18. Principle of restraint In ATU, Local 569 v. Edmonton (City), 2015 ABQB 620, Justice Renke stated that a principle of restraint should apply in the use of the court's contempt powers. His Lordship said: 89 Still there's a question of the conduct of the City in all of the circumstances. Again, the conduct of the City is nothing like the wild cat strikes of correctional workers. It was conduct based on understandable if legally irrelevant interests, and conduct that moved to resolve matters in a relatively brisk manner. Given that and given what I would call the principle of restraint or what Mr. Nugent referred to as a de minimis principle, should there be some latitude extended for what might technically be contempt, but which ought not to receive the label or stigma of being classified as contempt? 90 The principle of restraint isn't express in Canadian criminal law, or, so far as I know in US criminal law, although it is in some European systems. We do see the principle of restraint at work in legal rules like the de minimis rule. We also see it at work, for example, in the Mabior decision of the Supreme Court at paragraph 23 (2012 SCC 47) The court says there that “Morality infuses the criminal law. But the law does not seek to criminalize all immorality. The principal objective of the criminal law is the public identification of wrongdoing qua wrongdoing which violates public order and is so blameworthy that it deserves penal sanction.” I take this as an indication of the role of the principle of restraint in the criminal law. Since civil contempt is a quasi-criminal aspect of civil procedure, in my view, a principle of restraint ought to apply in the deployment of the contempt powers, as well. 19. Contempt Does Not Create a Cause of Action The sanctions for contempt are set out in rules 701–704 in the Alberta Rules of Court. The failure to obey a court order may be a breach of duty owed to the court but not the individual. A private cause of action does not arise as a result of a breach of the Rules of Court or a failure to exercise authority granted by reason of the court order. Contempt of court is not a tort, therefore the action against the individual police officers is struck. Gustavsen v. Calgary (City) (1996), 43 Alta. L.R. (3d) 13 (Master), at 17, per Master Alberstat. 20. Hearsay Evidence Not Permitted Moreover, the motion should be considered as a final order (and not an interlocutory order) and should not be based upon hearsay evidence. Kulyk v. Wigmore (1987), 53 Alta. L.R. (2d) 44 at 45 (C.A.). 21. Conflicting Affidavits Contempt hearings ought not to be decided on the basis of conflicting affidavits. In that case, viva voce evidence should be called. As for the argument that material facts in dispute ought not to be resolved by choice between conflicting affidavits, especially in a contempt hearing, we agree. It is true that the respondent is entitled to call viva voce evidence if he so requests if the affidavits filed “contain contradictory statements with respect to material facts or issues in the case”: R. v. B.E.S.T. Plating Shoppe Ltd. (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 145, (C.A.). Horrey v. Litterst (1995), 178 A.R. 216 (C.A.), at 219, per Fraser C.J.A. 22. Allegations against Lawyer Do not allege civil contempt of a lawyer without evidence. Therefore, upon the argument of the motion I dismissed the application in so far as an order had been sought citing the clerk of the court and Mr. Philion in civil contempt. Moreover, no evidence had been placed before the court to support the allegation that Mr. Philion had been in contempt of court. I said then and I repeat now, that it is unacceptable that an allegation be made formally in a court document that a barrister and solicitor is in civil contempt, an allegation which, while “civil”, is fundamentally criminal in nature, unless evidence is presented to the court, by affidavit or otherwise, in support of that allegation. A notice of motion making such an allegation ought not to be filed unless the applicant at the time of filing is in a position to support the allegation by affidavit. Counsel for Mr. Philion declined to ask for payment of costs, but if costs had been asked for they would have been awarded in favour of Mr. Philion in a substantial amount. Toronto Dominion Bank v. W-32 Corp. (1983), 27 Alta. L.R. (2d) 37 (Q.B.), at 39, per D.C. McDonald J. 23. Family Law Cases Are Treated Differently In ordinary civil law, it may be that mere breach of a court order is all that need be proved in order to establish contempt: Baxter Travenol Laboratories [of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Can.) Ltd. (1984), 14 D.L.R. (4th) 641 (F.C.T.D.)]. However, by long tradition, the court exercises restraint in family law cases. In custody cases, the court usually requires an intentional breach of the court order: [Gribben v. Gribben (1972), 9 R.F.L. 114 (B.C. S.C.); Sens v. Sens, [1974] 6 W.W.R. 667 (Sask. Q.B.); Singer v. Singer (1974), 17 R.F.L. 18 (Ont. H.C.)]. The reasoning in these cases, which reasoning I adopt, is that restraint is appropriate, given the twin objectives of protecting both the best interests of the children and the administration of justice. As frustrating as it must be for a parent whose court ordered access is sterilized, the court's focus is on the interests of the children, not on the behaviour of parents. Children are better off if their parents are not in jail or paying fines. Where the court can find that a parent is disobeying a court order out of honest concern for the welfare of the children, a court will be loathe to stigmatize and sanction the parent's behaviour. One test for the honest concern of the offending parent is whether that parent has promptly moved the court to modify the existing access or custody order. This higher threshold of personal culpability in breaching a court order before the court can declare contempt has been preserved in our Rules by the choice of the expression “adequate excuse”. Salloum v. Salloum (1994), 154 A.R. 65 (Q.B.), at 68–69, per Veit J. 24. Delay In Point on the Bow Development Ltd. v. William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd. (2006), 68 Alta. L.R. (4th) 308 (Alta. Q.B.); affirmed (2007) 78 Alta. L.R. (4th) 16 (Alta. C.A.)], Rooke J. made the following comments about delay: 115 It is to be hoped that future litigants, particularly those involved in case managed proceedings, will take some guidance from this case. Some of the points that I believe may provide guidance can be summarized to include: (1) a breach of a rule or enactment, which may merit a costs award, is not contempt in itself (in the absence of the Rule or enactment specifically so providing) unless so declared by the Court by a specific order or direction—rather any such breach should be subject to a specific Court order requiring compliance, the breach of which, without adequate excuse, would be, prima facie, contempt, confirmed upon further Court order; (2) whether conduct constitutes a contempt is a question of fact; (3) a party who causes delay and compels the other side to take motions to require compliance with the Rules, agreements and Court orders cannot be heard to complain that enforcement is delaying the case; (4) a party who feels aggrieved by the actions (or lack thereof) of another party that it considers to be contempt should seek a remedy in a timely fashion rather than accumulating grievances for a later contempt application; after all, contempt is not contempt inter partes, but contempt of court; (5) a party that finds itself unable to comply with an order or direction of the Court must act in advance to seek relief or must comply; (6) it is not an excuse for either party to say that nothing could be done because a case management justice was away; there are always alternatives available to allow issues to be dealt with expeditiously, including telephone conferences or reference of the matter to another justice pursuant to Rule 391, or to the Chief or Associate Chief Justice; (7) too much work for counsel is not an adequate excuse for failure to be timely in litigation—the answer is to get more help or have other counsel appointed; (8) if a motion is needed to compel someone to do something that they should have done in any event and they do it before the motion is heard, it is open to the applicant to continue the motion for the purpose of asking for costs thrown away, but this is not normally a matter of contempt; (9) absent relief by Court order, failure to conduct examinations for discovery within a Court- ordered time means that the party whose right it was to conduct the examinations has lost that right; (10) where there is disagreement between parties as to the terms of an order, the proper procedure is for counsel to arrange a hearing to settle the terms, rather than simply to act in disregard of the order; and (11) parties in case managed proceedings can and should resolve issues either as they arise or at the next case management meeting rather than saving them up for a future contempt battle. 25. Official in charge of government department In Ouellet v. M. (B.), 2010 ABCA 240, (sub nom. Alberta (Director of Child, Youth and Family Enhancement) v. M. (B.), 2010 CarswellAlta 1487, 8 Admin. L.R. (5th) 1, 2010 ABCA 240, 30 Alta. L.R. (5th) 42, 259 C.C.C. (3d) 154, 323 D.L.R. (4th) 745, 86 R.F.L. (6th) 1, [2010] 12 W.W.R. 232, 490 W.A.C. 273, the Alberta Court of Appeal had the following issue before it: Can liability for contempt of court be imposed personally on the holder of a public office who is in charge of a government department where the public officer is named as a party to an action and the department fails to obey a court order directing the public officer to act? The court stated, at para. 38: As already discussed, it is clear that in the appropriate circumstances, a government official can be held personally liable for the failure of his or her department to comply with a court order. Whether the department itself may also be held liable under Canadian law, as was suggested by the House of Lords in the Home Office case [M. v. Home Office, [1994] 1 A.C. 377], is not clear … The Court then said, at para. 41: However, it is unnecessary to opine on whether the office of the Director can or should be held liable … Nothing relieves Mr. Ouellet himself of responsibility. The facts are clear that Mr. Ouellet had a role to play in the response to the court order, having been advised by other members of the department on June 5 about the existence of the order. The law is clear that when an official in charge of a government department has the requisite knowledge, he or she can be found liable for contempt for the failure to comply with a court order.

Rule 10.52(3)(a)(i)—“other than an order for the payment of money” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. I think that it is plain that the intention of the drafter of R. 703(a) was to exclude from the scope of civil contempt any disobedience of an order for the payment of money, and that an order to pay maintenance in fixed amounts is “an order for the payment of money” within the meaning of R. 703(a). Craft v. Craft (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 223 (Q.B.), at 225, per D.C. McDonald J. In Dickie v. Dickie, 2007 SCC 8, 2007 CarswellOnt 606, [2007] 1 S.C.R. 346, the Court considered, among other things, Rule 60.11(1) of the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, which reads as follows: A contempt order to enforce an order requiring a person to do an act, other than the payment of money, or to abstain from doing an act, may be obtained only on motion to a judge in the proceeding in which the order to be enforced was made. A motions court ordered Mr. Dickie to pay support payments, and ordered him to secure those obligations by providing an irrevocable letter of credit and posting security for costs. When he did not do so, he was found to be in contempt. That finding of contempt was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal (Laskin J.A. dissenting) (see: (2006) 206 O.A.C. 257 (C.A.)). The Supreme Court of Canada allowed the appeal and reinstated the finding of contempt. With respect to the submission that the order to post a letter of credit was really an order to pay money, the Supreme Court of Canada said, at paragraph 7, that it was “in substantial agreement with the reasons of Laskin, J.A.” Laskin J.A. said, at paragraph 104 (O.A.C.): I accept that an irrevocable letter of credit is “money or money's worth,“and that an order to post security for costs ordinarily is satisfied by the payment of money. However, to determine whether an order is an order for the payment of money under r. 60.11(1), one must consider to whom the money is being paid and the effect of the order for payment. Where money is ordered to be paid not to the creditor but into court—or its functional equivalent, to a solicitor to be held in trust—and where the effect of the order is not to create a fixed debt obligation but to secure a debt obligation, then the order is not an order for the payment of money under r. 60.11(1). In Mella v. 336239 Alberta Ltd., 2016 ABCA 226, 2016 CarswellAlta 1409, Mella was a judgment debtor of 336239 Alberta Ltd. (operating as “Dave's Diesel”). Dave's Diesel obtained an attachment order “directing [Mella] to limit their monthly expenditures … and to provide detailed monthly expenditure records”. Mella was found in contempt of that order “because he had unlawfully used more money than permitted and had failed to provide adequate expenditure records” (the first contempt order). Mella was subsequently found in contempt (the second contempt order) for continuing contempt under the first contempt order, and for evading lawful enforcement proceedings. The Court of Queen's Bench imposed monetary sanctions (a payment to Dave's Diesel equal to what was spent in contravention of the attachment order, payment of two fines, and payment of Dave's Diesel solicitor-client costs). The contempt under the second contempt order was not purged and Mella was imprisoned. Mella sought a stay of the second contempt order. One of the grounds for the stay application was that failure to pay money is not contempt. In dismissing the stay application, Schutz, J.A. said: 22 … fines imposed for contempt of court are an obligation owing to the court, separate from the civil action in which it arises: SNC-Lavalin Profac Inc v Sankar, 2009 ONCA 97 at paras 14-17, 94 OR (3d) 236; Sussex Group Ltd v 3933938 Canada Inc., 2003 CanLII 49334 at para 13 (Ont SC). Sometimes, it is appropriate to direct payment of fines for contempt to other than the Clerk of the Court: MEL(P) v BJL, 2013 ABQB 227, 560 AR 165; Berube v Wingrowich, 2003 ABQB 805, 24 Alta LR (4th) 398; Alberta Treasury Branches v Chocolaterie Bernard Callebaut Partnership, 2012 ABQB 245. 23 Two types of judgments or orders direct a person to pay money: those which direct a person to pay money to another person and those which direct a person to pay money into court. 24 It is not Mella's failure to pay his civil debt to Dave's Diesel that underlies the contempt sanctions imposed; rather, his misconduct in continuing to flagrantly breach the court's orders is the reason contempt sanctions have been imposed. The First Contempt Order found that Mella had defied a court-ordered injunction prohibiting him from exceeding a stipulated expenditure limit on household expenditures, and he had also failed to provide ordered financial records. 25 Rule 10.52(3)(a)(i) refers only to the payment of money. But, the rule does not exclude the use of the contempt power to punish Mella for defiance of, and to coerce his compliance with, a mandatory injunction explicitly limiting his household expenditures and requiring a proper accounting, nor does it preclude disgorgement as sanction. It is not determinative that the First Contempt Order requires that money or money's worth be paid because a court order that punishes and coerces is not the functional equivalent of payment by Mella to Dave's Diesel for ordinary debts—a critical distinction: Dickie v Dickie (2006), 78 OR (3d) 1 at para 103, 262 DLR (4th) 622 at paras 105–116 (Laskin JA), affd 2007 SCC 8, [2007] 1 SCR 346. Moreover, the First Contempt Order subsists unencumbered by appeal or variation. 26 Rule 10.53 expressly authorizes the imposition of fines, imprisonment and costs. 27 Fines and imprisonment are means of enforcing “compliance with the process of the court itself”: Johnson v Schwalm, 2006 CanLII 13771 at para 24, 2006 CarswellOnt 2620. Mella's imprisonment serves both as punishment and an incentive to purge his ongoing contempt: Korea Data Systems Co v Chiang, 2007 ONCA 529 at para 11, 77 CPC (6th) 253. 28 Apart from arguing that the court below miscalculated cumulative amounts owing, and mis-characterized the nature of some payments he did make, Mella does not challenge the court's extant authority to levy fines, or to make imprisonment a sanction for civil contempt. Mella has not demonstrated any error by the court below in its calculations, or characterizations, or in imposing monetary sanctions. 29 As for costs, sound public policy underlies the imposition of a costs order: it is the contemnors who ought to bear a substantial portion of the costs directly relating to their contempt, as this brings home the seriousness of their action and their responsibility for the consequences of their contempt: Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2005 ABCA 185 at para 11, 371 AR 11. As defined in the Rules of Court, a “costs award” includes “the amount payable by one party to another in accordance with … r 10.31”, and can form part of a penalty for contempt of court: Richards v Richards, 2013 ABQB 484 at para 147, 568 AR 302.

Sloppy Practice Is Not Contempt See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Miller v. 32807 Alberta Ltd. (1986), 70 A.R. 303 (C.A.), the defendant had failed to provide adequate responses to undertakings given at discovery (as required by an order). At p. 304 the court said: Material before the learned chambers judge was, to say the least, skimpy There were responses given to the underakings. The plaintiff (respondent) considered those responses to be inadequate in the sense that “clarification” was required. Reviewing the material before the chambers judge it would be impossible to say whether the order had been complied with. We are told that the chambers judge expressed grave concern about the failure of the defendant's solicitor to respond to the correspondence about the clarification. Those facts would not, however, justify this order on this notice of motion. Striking out a defence and permitting a default judgment is a drastic remedy, for what is, is reality, sloppy and unacceptable practice as distinct from contempt.

Rule 10.52(3)(a)(vi)—Implied undertakings See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Jutte v. Jutte (2007), 77 Alta. L.R. (4th) 126 (Alta. Q.B.), Brooker J. found that the plaintiff's lawyer (Mr. Sproule) had breached his implied undertaking of confidentiality arising from an examination for discovery. In declining to find that the breach constituted contempt of court, his Lordship said, at p. 138: 41 The foregoing cases demonstrate that knowledge of the existence of the court order that has allegedly been breached is a necessary precondition to a finding of contempt, although it may not always be necessary to prove that the defaulter intended to breach the order. 42 In this case, having regard to my previous findings, I am satisfied that the implied undertaking exists and that Sproule breached the implied undertaking. His defence is that he was not aware of the implied undertaking. His counsel argues that the implied undertaking rule is not found in the Alberta Rules of Court nor the Alberta Evidence Act, R.S.A. 2000 c. A-18. While that may be so, I note that the genesis of the rule is certainly found in the Alberta Code of Professional Conduct as referred to earlier. Does ignorance an of the implied undertaking provide a reasonable excuse for the breach? 43 With some reluctance, I hold that it does. The essence of contempt is deliberate conduct in breach of a court order or undertaking. Obviously, if someone is to be found guilty of breach of a court order, it must be shown that the offender had knowledge of that order. How else could he be expected to govern his conduct accordingly? This is no doubt why the courts are vigilant in proceedings to hold someone in contempt of a court order to ensure that there is adequate proof that the respondent has been properly served with the order. With respect to proceedings for breach of a specific undertaking to the court, one would expect the applicant to begin by proving that the respondent had given the undertaking that he has allegedly breached. By doing so, the respondent's knowledge of the existence of the undertaking is proved. 44 However, with respect to the implied undertaking here, Sproule has not given anything specifically to the court. Rather, he is presumed, as a matter of law, to have given it. He specifically denies knowing of the existence of the implied undertaking. Is that a reasonable excuse for its breach? Given the potential serious consequences which can flow from a finding of contempt of court I hold that it is. Sloppy practice is not contempt of court: Miller v. 32807 Alberta Ltd. (1986), 70 A.R. 303 (C.A.).

commentary.text:
Rule 10.52(3) sets out a number of grounds on which a person may be found in civil contempt, including not complying with an order, engaging in conduct warranting a declaration of contempt, refusing to answer proper questions at trial or failing to perform or observe an undertaking given to the court – all on condition that such conduct is “without reasonable excuse”. In addition, in proper cases, contempt may be declared even when a person does not fit within the enumerated categories because contempt of court is an inherent remedy. Kent v. Martin Braun (Re) , [2012] A.J. No. 758, 2012 ABQB 467 at para. 21 (Alta. Q.B.), citing , The rule does not exclude the use of the contempt power to punish for defiance of, and to coerce compliance with, a mandatory injunction explicitly limiting household expenditures and requiring a proper accounting, nor does it preclude disgorgement as sanction. 336239 Alberta Ltd. (c.o.b. Dave’s Diesel Repair) v. Mella, [2016] A.J. No. 763, 2016 ABCA 226 at para. 25 (Alta. C.A.).
Rule 10.53 expressly authorizes the imposition of fines, imprisonment and costs. 336239 Alberta Ltd. (c.o.b. Dave’s Diesel Repair) v. Mella, [2016] A.J. No. 763, 2016 ABCA 226 at para. 26 (Alta. C.A.).
Contempt for Breach of Orders The following summary is largely taken from , [2023] A.J. No. 1224, 2023 Martineau v. Espina ABKB 664 at paras. 12-18 (Alta. K.B.). – Legal authorities have settled “that all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has [2006] A.J. No. 52, 2006 ABCA 23 (Alta. C.A.).

(1) Except when a person is before the Court as described in subrule (3)(a)(ii) or (v), before an order declaring a person in civil contempt of Court is made, notice of the application in Form 27 for a declaration of civil contempt must be served on the person in the same manner as a commencement document.
